## Iowa Lead Azide Detonation: 4,500 kg Destroyed | World News, Nov 25

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/world-today-2026-11-25-h/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvbJjw6NrsQ
Published: 2026-11-26 · Duration: 1:54 · Place: Middletown
Short answer: The US Army destroyed about 4,500 kilograms of degraded lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant, and early EPA readings showed no airborne lead.

The November 25 world news briefing maps a fuel truck fire that killed at least 31 people in Cairo, Brazil's response to new US tariffs on aircraft and sugar, and Poland's plan for a no-fly zone on its border with Ukraine. It also covers a South African court ruling on the Phala Phala report and North Korea's closure of Switzerland's office in Pyongyang.

Key facts:
- United States · Iowa: Army detonates unstable explosive (The degraded explosive risked going off on its own as temperatures dropped, so about 4,500 kilograms were destroyed.) [source: AL JAZEERA · FRANCE 24 (AP)]
- Brazil · Trade: Brazil rejects new us tariff plan (That includes a 10 percent duty on finished planes made by Embraer.) [source: AL JAZEERA · AGÊNCIA BRASIL]
- Poland · Defence: Poland plans border no-fly zone (Deputy minister Cezary Tomczyk said it would help pilots down Russian missiles and drones.) [source: KYIV INDEP. · NOTES FROM POLAND]
- South Africa · Courts: Court voids phala phala report (Judges in Cape Town set aside a 2022 panel report that paved the way to impeachment.) [source: EWN · AL JAZEERA (REUTERS, AP)]
- Egypt · Cairo: Fuel truck fire kills 31 in cairo (Egypt's health ministry says at least 31 people were killed.) [source: AL JAZEERA · FRANCE 24 (AFP)]
- North Korea · Switzerland: North korea shuts swiss office (State media say the Swiss envoy had 48 hours to leave.) [source: AL JAZEERA · NK NEWS]

### World news on the map: 25 November 2026

The international headlines of 25 November 2026, mapped from west to east.

## United States · Iowa: Army detonates unstable explosive

We start in Iowa, where the US Army blew up its stockpile of lead azide. The degraded explosive risked going off on its own as temperatures dropped, so about 4,500 kilograms were destroyed. Early EPA readings showed no airborne lead, but some residents fear lasting contamination.

## Brazil · Trade: Brazil rejects new us tariff plan

Now to Brazil, where Washington proposed new tariffs on aircraft and sugar. That includes a 10 percent duty on finished planes made by Embraer. President Lula's office called the move unacceptable. It wants a negotiated deal, but does not rule out reciprocal measures.

## Poland · Defence: Poland plans border no-fly zone

Now Poland, which plans a no-fly zone along its eastern border with Ukraine. Deputy minister Cezary Tomczyk said it would help pilots down Russian missiles and drones. He hopes it will be in place by early January. Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski calls downing missiles over Ukraine self-defence; NATO is not in favour.

## South Africa · Courts: Court voids phala phala report

In South Africa, President Cyril Ramaphosa won a court ruling on Wednesday. Judges in Cape Town set aside a 2022 panel report that paved the way to impeachment. It concerned cash stolen from his farm; the court said the panel overstepped. That halts the impeachment inquiry based on it.

## Egypt · Cairo: Fuel truck fire kills 31 in cairo

Then Cairo, where a fuel truck overturned and burst into flames on the Ring Road. Egypt's health ministry says at least 31 people were killed. Prosecutors say 27 vehicles burned and have opened an investigation. Footage showed a huge fireball over the Al-Warraq neighbourhood.

## North Korea · Switzerland: North korea shuts swiss office

Finally, Pyongyang, where North Korea has shut Switzerland's new diplomatic office. State media say the Swiss envoy had 48 hours to leave. The row is over Swiss sanctions on a children's camp; Bern regrets the move and is sending its envoy to Beijing.

FAQ:

## Did the Korean War Ever Really End?

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/korea-38/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=glrslVz1Xrs
Published: 2026-11-25 · Duration: 0:39 · Place: Korean Demilitarized Zone
Short answer: Did the Korean War ever really end? The fighting stopped on 27 July 1953 with an armistice, a military ceasefire, but no peace treaty has ever been signed. And the border it left isn't the 38th parallel: it's where the front line froze.

Key facts:
- 38th parallel proposed: 10–11 August 1945 (Two US colonels, Charles Bonesteel and Dean Rusk, proposed the line overnight at the Pentagon.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- War begins: 25 June 1950 (North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel.) [source: United Nations Command]
- Armistice signed: 27 July 1953 (Signed at 10:00 at Panmunjom; it came into force at 22:00 the same day.) [source: US National Archives]
- Signatories: U.N. Command, North Korea, China (The armistice is a military agreement; South Korea did not sign it.) [source: BBC]
- Peace treaty: None signed (A permanent peace treaty has never been signed, so the peninsula technically remains in a state of war.) [source: United Nations Command]
- Width of the DMZ: 4 km (The Demilitarized Zone extends 2 km on each side of the Military Demarcation Line.) [source: US National Archives]
- Border vs. 38th parallel: Crosses it (The 1953 line runs south of the parallel in the west and north of it in the east.)

### Why the Korean War Is Still Only on Pause

The Korean War has been on pause since 1953. The fighting stopped on 27 July 1953 with an armistice, a military ceasefire, but no peace treaty has ever been signed. The border it left behind is not the 38th parallel either: it is the line where the front froze.

## Where did the 38th parallel come from?

In August 1945, as the Second World War was ending, Korea was split in two at the 38th parallel. The line was proposed on the night of 10 to 11 August 1945 by two US colonels, Charles Bonesteel and Dean Rusk, working at the Pentagon. According to Rusk's memorandum, the aim was to include the capital of Korea in the area of responsibility of American troops.

Under General Order No. 1, approved on 15 August 1945, the United States would accept the Japanese surrender south of the parallel and the Soviet Union north of it. Soviet troops reached the line later that month; American troops landed in September.

## How did the Korean War start?

On 25 June 1950, North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel. What followed was a war of movement:

- **Summer 1950**: the front swung south, down to the Pusan perimeter.
- **Autumn 1950**: after the Inchon landing on 15 September, the front swung north, close to the Yalu River.
- **Winter 1950 to 1951**: after China intervened on 25 October 1950, the front moved back south, and Seoul fell again on 4 January 1951.

From mid-1951, the front settled near the 38th parallel, and it stayed there for the rest of the war.

## Did the Korean War ever end?

The fighting ended. The war, formally, did not. On 27 July 1953 an armistice was signed at **Panmunjom**, at 10:00, and it came into force at 22:00 that night.

It was signed by Lieutenant General William K. Harrison Jr. for the United Nations Command and General Nam Il for the Korean People's Army and the Chinese People's Volunteers. In short: **North Korea, China and the U.N. Command signed it. South Korea did not.** Its president at the time, Syngman Rhee, refused.

The armistice is a military document. Its own text calls for a cessation of hostilities "until a final peaceful settlement is achieved". That settlement never came: a conference in Geneva in 1954 failed, and according to the United Nations Command, a permanent peace treaty has never been signed, so the Korean Peninsula technically remains in a state of war.

The question is still open. In August 2026, South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, proposed talks "to officially end the war".

## Is the border between North and South Korea the 38th parallel?

No. The border set in 1953 is not the 1945 line: it is where the front stood when the fighting stopped.

That line **crosses** the 38th parallel rather than following it. In the west, it runs south of the parallel, so the city of Kaesong, which lies south of the 38th, ended up in North Korea. In the east, the border runs north of the parallel, so a mountainous area above the 38th belongs to South Korea.

## What is the DMZ?

Around the line runs the **Demilitarized Zone**, or DMZ. It is 4 kilometres wide: 2 kilometres on each side of the Military Demarcation Line, the line where the front froze in 1953. It still separates the two Koreas today.

## Key takeaways

- Korea was split at the 38th parallel in August 1945, on a line proposed by two US officers.
- The Korean War began on 25 June 1950, when North Korean forces crossed the parallel.
- An armistice stopped the fighting on 27 July 1953; North Korea, China and the U.N. Command signed it, South Korea did not.
- No peace treaty has ever been signed, so the war is on pause rather than formally over.
- Today's border is the 1953 front line, which crosses the 38th parallel, surrounded by a 4 km wide DMZ.

FAQ:
Q: Is the Korean War still going on?
A: The fighting stopped on 27 July 1953 with an armistice, but no peace treaty has ever been signed. According to the United Nations Command, the Korean Peninsula technically remains in a state of war.
Q: Who signed the Korean War armistice?
A: The armistice was signed by the United Nations Command, North Korea and China at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. South Korea did not sign it.
Q: Is the North Korea–South Korea border the 38th parallel?
A: No. The border is the front line where the fighting stopped in 1953, and it crosses the 38th parallel: it runs south of it in the west and north of it in the east.

Transcript:

Rewind to 1945. Korea is split in two at the 38th parallel.
In June 1950, North Korean troops cross it.
The front swings south… north… and back.
July 1953: an armistice. The fighting stops.
North Korea, China and the U.N. Command sign it. South Korea doesn't.
The new border isn't the parallel. It's where the front froze.
Around it: the DMZ, four kilometres wide.
And still, no peace treaty. Which means…

Sources: United Nations Command; US National Archives; US Office of the Historian; BBC; Reuters

## Chile Is Longer Than Lisbon to Moscow

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/chile-length/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rhv_-F-Rd40
Published: 2026-11-24 · Duration: 0:40 · Place: Chile
Short answer: How long is Chile? 4,270 km from north to south, but only 177 km wide on average. Lay it over Europe with its southern tip on Lisbon and it doesn't stop at Moscow: it keeps going for another 360 km, crossing ten countries on the way.

Key facts:
- Length of Chile: 4,270 km (Measured from north to south along the country.) [source: Library of Congress, Chile: A Country Study]
- Average width of Chile: 177 km (Chile is more than 24 times longer than it is wide on average.) [source: Library of Congress, Chile: A Country Study]
- Lisbon to Moscow: 3,907 km (The straight-line distance between the two capitals.)
- Distance past Moscow: About 360 km (With its southern tip on Lisbon, Chile's northern tip lands about 360 km beyond Moscow.) [source: outline measured and placed on Natural Earth]
- Countries crossed in Europe: 10 (Russia, Germany, France, Belarus, Poland, Lithuania, Portugal, Spain, Belgium and the Netherlands.) [source: outline measured and placed on Natural Earth]
- Europe from west to east: About 5,200–5,460 km (From Cabo da Roca in Portugal to the Urals, so Europe is still wider than Chile is long.)

### Laying Chile Over Europe: A Country Longer Than Lisbon to Moscow

Chile is 4,270 km long from north to south, yet on average only 177 km wide. Lay it over Europe with its southern tip on Lisbon and it does not stop at Moscow, 3,907 km away: it keeps going for about another 360 km, passing over ten countries on the way.

## How long is Chile?

Chile measures 4,270 km from its northern border to its southern tip, according to the Library of Congress country study. Its average width is just 177 km, and even at its widest it reaches only about 350 km.

That shape is hard to grasp on a normal map, where Chile looks like a thin ribbon and is easy to dismiss as small. Its length tells a different story.

## What happens if you put Chile over Europe?

To make that length easier to picture, we took Chile's real outline and moved it across the Atlantic without stretching it, then laid it over Europe.

- Its **southern tip** lands on Lisbon.
- From there it climbs through Galicia in Spain, crosses Brittany in France, then Belgium and northern Germany.
- It continues over Poland and Belarus.
- It passes **right over Moscow**.
- Then it keeps going for **about 360 km** beyond the Russian capital.

The outline is not a straight line. Chile is slightly arched, so when it lies across Europe it bends north through Galicia, Brittany and Belgium instead of following the straight route from Lisbon to Moscow.

Along the way, the cities that fall inside the outline include Lisbon, Cologne, Berlin, Vilnius, Minsk, Moscow and Vladimir.

## How many countries does Chile cover in Europe?

Ten. Measured on Natural Earth outlines, Chile's shape covers part of Russia (including Kaliningrad), Germany, France, Belarus, Poland, Lithuania, Portugal, Spain, Belgium and the Netherlands.

That is ten European countries sitting under one long, thin South American country.

## Is Chile longer than Lisbon to Moscow?

Yes. The straight-line distance from Lisbon to Moscow is 3,907 km. Chile is 4,270 km long, so the difference is about 360 km. When we placed Chile's outline on the map, its northern tip ended up just over 360 km past Moscow, which matches the official figures.

## Is Chile longer than Europe is wide?

No, and this is a claim worth correcting. Measured from Cabo da Roca in Portugal to the Ural Mountains, Europe spans roughly 5,200 to 5,460 km, depending on where along the Urals you stop. Chile, at 4,270 km, is shorter than that.

So Chile does not stretch across all of Europe. But it is easily longer than the trip from Lisbon to Moscow, which is already a very long way.

## Key takeaways

- Chile is 4,270 km long and only 177 km wide on average.
- Laid over Europe from Lisbon, it passes over Moscow and continues about 360 km further.
- The straight-line distance from Lisbon to Moscow is 3,907 km.
- Chile's outline covers ten European countries, from Portugal to Russia.
- Europe, at about 5,200 to 5,460 km from west to east, is still wider than Chile is long.

FAQ:
Q: How long is Chile in km?
A: Chile is 4,270 km long from north to south, but only 177 km wide on average.
Q: Is Chile longer than the distance from Lisbon to Moscow?
A: Yes. Lisbon to Moscow is 3,907 km in a straight line, while Chile is 4,270 km long. With its southern tip on Lisbon, Chile would reach about 360 km past Moscow.
Q: Is Chile longer than Europe is wide?
A: No. Europe measures roughly 5,200 to 5,460 km from Cabo da Roca in Portugal to the Urals, while Chile is 4,270 km long. Chile is, however, longer than the distance from Lisbon to Moscow.

Russia: Wait. It's still going?

Sources: Library of Congress, Chile: A Country Study; outline measured and placed on Natural Earth

## Nvidia Brings Back Jensen Huang | World News, Nov 23

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/world-today-2026-11-23-h/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0OTg5656th8
Published: 2026-11-24 · Duration: 1:59 · Place: Santa Clara
Short answer: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, and its shares closed more than 31% higher on Monday.

The November 23 world news briefing maps NATO's AWACS decision for Poland after the Kh-101 missile crashes, Ukraine's claim that it sank the Russian corvette Merkury in Benghazi and the drone attack on a police base in Cúcuta. It also covers India's $1.6bn package for Nepal, the candy factory fire in Indonesia and the air-raid alert on South Korea's Ulleung Island.

Key facts:
- United States · Tech: Nvidia reinstates jensen huang (The board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang, who resigned on November 12.) [source: NVIDIA · BBC]
- Colombia · Security: Drones hit police base in cúcuta (Explosive drones targeted the regional police command before dawn on Monday.) [source: EFE · CARACOL RADIO]
- Poland · Nato: Nato sends awacs to poland (Polish prosecutors say three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles came down on Friday.) [source: REUTERS · POLSKIE RADIO]
- Libya · Ukraine War: Ukraine claims warship sunk (Ukraine's president says seven Ukrainian-made sea drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury there on Sunday.) [source: ABC NEWS · CNBC]
- India · Nepal: India pledges $1.6bn to nepal (Narendra Modi announced it after talks with Nepal's new prime minister, Balendra Shah.) [source: BBC · HINDUSTAN TIMES]
- Indonesia · Factory Fire: 24 dead in candy factory fire (Officials confirmed on Monday that 24 people died in a fire at a candy factory in Cikande.) [source: REUTERS · XINHUA]
- South Korea · Air Defence: Russian jets trigger island alert (Seoul says Russian warplanes entered its air defence zone early Tuesday, local time, and neared Ulleung Island.) [source: YONHAP · KOREA TIMES]

### World news on the map: 23 November 2026

The international headlines of 23 November 2026, mapped from west to east.

## United States · Tech: Nvidia reinstates jensen huang

We start in Santa Clara, California, where Nvidia brought back its chief executive. The board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang, who resigned on November 12. Nvidia shares closed more than 31 percent higher on Monday. The board says an independent investigation will continue.

## Colombia · Security: Drones hit police base in cúcuta

Now to Cúcuta, in northeastern Colombia, near the border with Venezuela. Explosive drones targeted the regional police command before dawn on Monday. Officials say no officers were hurt, but three civilians, including a baby, were injured. More than 60 homes were damaged.

## Poland · Nato: Nato sends awacs to poland

Then Poland, where NATO is answering missiles that crashed inside the country. Polish prosecutors say three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles came down on Friday. After a NATO meeting on Monday, Poland said allies will provide an AWACS early-warning plane. It helps detect low-flying missiles and drones.

## Libya · Ukraine War: Ukraine claims warship sunk

South to Benghazi, in eastern Libya. Ukraine's president says seven Ukrainian-made sea drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury there on Sunday. He says a helicopter on board was destroyed and a Russian cargo ship was hit. The UN mission in Libya called for an independent investigation.

## India · Nepal: India pledges $1.6bn to nepal

In New Delhi, India pledged 1.6 billion dollars to Nepal. Narendra Modi announced it after talks with Nepal's new prime minister, Balendra Shah. Nepal had asked for two billion, after floods that killed more than 1,400 people. India also agreed to give Nepal access to two more ports.

## Indonesia · Factory Fire: 24 dead in candy factory fire

Now to Indonesia, west of Jakarta, in Banten province. Officials confirmed on Monday that 24 people died in a fire at a candy factory in Cikande. About 30 workers are still missing. Early reports point to a short circuit in an air conditioner.

## South Korea · Air Defence: Russian jets trigger island alert

Last stop: South Korea, where an island got an air-raid alert. Seoul says Russian warplanes entered its air defence zone early Tuesday, local time, and neared Ulleung Island. Fighter jets scrambled; the alert lasted minutes. Seoul says its airspace was not violated, and will protest to Russia.

## Why Is Norway Richer Than Sweden?

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/norway-sweden/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QrwMeYyM95I
Published: 2026-11-23 · Duration: 0:40 · Place: Ekofisk, North Sea
Short answer: Why is Norway so rich? In 1970 Sweden was 44% richer per person. Then the North Sea was split down the middle in 1965, Ekofisk was found on Norway's side in 1969, and Norway taxed the oil and saved it abroad: a fund now worth over $2 trillion.

Key facts:
- GDP per person in 1970: Sweden $4,729 · Norway $3,291 (In current US dollars, Sweden was about 44% richer per person than Norway.) [source: World Bank]
- GDP per person in 2024: Norway $89,889 · Sweden $57,223 (In current US dollars. The order flipped in the decades after North Sea oil.) [source: World Bank]
- Norway's geologists on offshore oil: 1958: ruled out (The Geological Survey of Norway wrote to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that finding coal, oil or sulphur on the continental shelf could be discounted.) [source: Norwegian Petroleum (Norsk Petroleum)]
- North Sea split by the median line: 1965 (Agreements with the United Kingdom (March) and Denmark (December) divided the continental shelf along the median line.) [source: Norwegian Petroleum (Norsk Petroleum)]
- Ekofisk discovered: Late 1969 (Phillips Petroleum reported it just before Christmas. One of the largest offshore oil fields ever discovered; production began on 15 June 1971.) [source: Norwegian Petroleum (Norsk Petroleum)]
- Marginal tax rate on oil profits: 78% (The ordinary 22% company tax plus a special petroleum tax.) [source: Norwegian Petroleum (Norsk Petroleum)]
- Norway's oil fund (30 September 2026): NOK 22,014 billion (About $2.3 trillion. The fund invests only abroad, so the Norwegian economy does not overheat.) [source: Norges Bank Investment Management]

### Why Norway Became Richer Than Sweden

Norway is richer than Sweden today because of the sea off its coast and what it did with what was found there. In 1970 Sweden was the richer neighbour: $4,729 of GDP per person against Norway's $3,291, about 44% more. In 1965 the North Sea floor was divided along the median line, in late 1969 the giant Ekofisk field was found on Norway's side, and Norway taxed the oil heavily and saved the money abroad. By 2024 Norway's GDP per person was $89,889 and Sweden's $57,223.

## Was Sweden really richer than Norway?

Yes. World Bank figures in current US dollars put Sweden's GDP per person at $4,729 in 1970 and Norway's at $3,291. Sweden had a large industrial base and was one of the richest countries in Europe. Norway was a smaller economy built on shipping, fishing and hydropower.

Nobody expected that to change. In 1958 the Geological Survey of Norway wrote to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that the possibility of finding coal, oil or sulphur on the continental shelf off the Norwegian coast could be discounted.

## How was the North Sea divided?

The discovery of the Groningen gas field in the Netherlands in 1959 changed minds about the North Sea. In May 1963 Norway proclaimed sovereignty over its continental shelf, and in 1965 it signed agreements with the United Kingdom and Denmark that drew the boundaries on the basis of the median line: a line halfway between the coasts.

That simple rule mattered enormously. It gave Norway a large share of the central and northern North Sea, including the area where Ekofisk would later be found.

## What was Ekofisk?

Norway's first licensing round was announced on 13 April 1965. The first exploration well, drilled in the summer of 1966, was dry. Then, just before Christmas 1969, Phillips Petroleum told the Norwegian authorities it had found Ekofisk, which turned out to be one of the largest offshore oil fields ever discovered. Production started on 15 June 1971, and a series of major discoveries followed in the next few years.

Ekofisk lies in block 2/4, in the Norwegian sector, close to the median line with the United Kingdom.

## How did Norway keep the money?

Norway made sure that a large share of the value went to the state. Oil companies pay the ordinary company tax plus a special petroleum tax, for a combined marginal rate of 78% on oil profits.

The surplus goes into the Government Pension Fund Global, often called the oil fund. It invests only abroad, so that the money does not overheat the Norwegian economy. At the end of September 2026 it was worth 22,014 billion kroner, around $2.3 trillion.

## So was it luck or policy?

Both parts are true. The oil was under the seabed whether anyone looked or not, and the median line put the biggest early field on Norway's side. But the decisions about how to tax the oil and where to put the money were made by Norway, and they are why the windfall turned into lasting wealth.

Sweden is still one of the richest countries in the world. The difference is that, since the 1970s, Norway has had a second engine its neighbour does not have.

FAQ:
Q: Why is Norway richer than Sweden?
A: Mainly North Sea oil. The seabed was split along the median line in 1965, the Ekofisk field was found on Norway's side in 1969, and Norway taxed the oil at a 78% marginal rate and saved the surplus abroad in its oil fund.
Q: Was Sweden ever richer than Norway?
A: Yes. In 1970 Sweden's GDP per person was $4,729 and Norway's $3,291 (World Bank, current US$), so Sweden was about 44% richer per person.
Q: How big is Norway's oil fund?
A: On 30 September 2026 it was worth 22,014 billion Norwegian kroner, around $2.3 trillion, according to Norges Bank Investment Management.
Q: Where is the Ekofisk oil field?
A: In block 2/4 of the Norwegian sector of the North Sea, close to the median line with the United Kingdom.

And in 1969, just before Christmas: Ekofisk.
One of the biggest offshore oil fields ever found, on Norway's side.
Norway taxed the oil hard, and invested the money abroad.
Today, that fund is worth over two trillion dollars.
So was it luck, or smart policy?

Sources: World Bank (GDP per capita, current US$); Norwegian Petroleum (Norsk Petroleum); Norges Bank Investment Management; Marine Regions (VLIZ)

## Kaliningrad: Why Does Russia Own It?

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/kaliningrad/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SJb-IVBDslA
Published: 2026-11-23 · Duration: 0:41 · Place: Kaliningrad Oblast
Short answer: Why does Russia own Kaliningrad, a piece of land squeezed between Poland and Lithuania, inside the EU and NATO and two countries away from the rest of Russia? We rewind to 1945, when it was still the German city of Königsberg.

Key facts:
- Former name: Königsberg (Until 1945 the city was German, part of East Prussia.)
- Transferred to the USSR: 1945 (The Potsdam Agreement of August 1, 1945 placed Königsberg and the northern part of East Prussia under the Soviet Union.) [source: Potsdam Agreement (1945)]
- Renamed Kaliningrad: July 4, 1946 (The city was renamed after Mikhail Kalinin.)
- Cut off from mainland Russia: 1991 (The USSR recognised Lithuania's independence on September 6, 1991, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved in December 1991.)
- Neighbours in NATO and the EU: By 2004 (Poland joined NATO in 1999 and Lithuania on March 29, 2004; both joined the EU on May 1, 2004.) [source: NATO and EU accession records]
- Ice-free port: Baltiysk (Home of Russia's Baltic Fleet and Russia's only Baltic port that stays free of ice all year.) [source: US Naval Institute]
- Area and population: About 15,100 km² · about 1 million people (A small exclave compared with the rest of Russia.)

### How Kaliningrad Became a Piece of Russia Outside Russia

Russia owns Kaliningrad because the Soviet Union took over the area at the end of World War II, when it was the German city of Königsberg. When the USSR collapsed in 1991 and Lithuania became independent, Kaliningrad stayed with Russia but was left cut off from the rest of the country. Today it sits between Poland and Lithuania, both members of NATO and the EU.

## Where is Kaliningrad?

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, squeezed between **Poland** and **Lithuania**. It covers about 15,100 km² and is home to about one million people.

It does not touch the rest of Russia. To reach mainland Russia over land, you have to cross at least two countries: Lithuania and then Belarus or Latvia.

## Was Kaliningrad always Russian?

No. Until 1945 it was German. The city was called **Königsberg**, and the surrounding region was the northern part of East Prussia.

At the end of World War II, the **Potsdam Agreement** of August 1, 1945 placed Königsberg and northern East Prussia under the Soviet Union. On July 4, 1946, the city was renamed **Kaliningrad**, after Mikhail Kalinin.

## Why is Kaliningrad separated from Russia?

For decades the separation hardly mattered on the map, because the land between Kaliningrad and Russia was all part of the Soviet Union, Lithuania included.

That changed in 1991. The USSR recognised Lithuania's independence on **September 6, 1991**, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved in December of that year. Kaliningrad remained part of the new Russian Federation, but there was now an independent country between it and the rest of Russia. The exclave was cut off.

## Is Kaliningrad surrounded by NATO and the EU?

Yes. Poland joined NATO in 1999, and Lithuania joined on **March 29, 2004**. Both countries joined the European Union on **May 1, 2004**. So by 2004, both of Kaliningrad's neighbours were in NATO and the EU.

## Why does Russia keep Kaliningrad?

One key reason is its coastline. The port of **Baltiysk**, in the Kaliningrad region, is the base of Russia's Baltic Fleet. It is Russia's only port on the Baltic Sea that stays free of ice all year round, according to the US Naval Institute and DW.

That makes the exclave valuable even though it is physically separated from the rest of the country.

## What is an exclave?

An exclave is a piece of a country that is cut off from its main territory by other countries. Kaliningrad fits that description exactly: it is Russian land, but the rest of Russia is two countries away.

The borders that created it were drawn in two steps. First, in 1945, the region passed from Germany to the Soviet Union. Then, in 1991, the Soviet Union broke apart, and the land between Kaliningrad and Russia became part of independent Lithuania.

## Key takeaways

- Kaliningrad was the German city of Königsberg until 1945.
- The Potsdam Agreement placed it under the Soviet Union, and it was renamed Kaliningrad on July 4, 1946.
- When the USSR collapsed in 1991 and Lithuania became independent, Kaliningrad was cut off from mainland Russia.
- By 2004, its neighbours Poland and Lithuania were both in NATO and the EU.
- Baltiysk is Russia's only Baltic port that never freezes, and the base of the Baltic Fleet.

FAQ:
Q: Why does Russia own Kaliningrad?
A: Russia owns Kaliningrad because the Potsdam Agreement of 1945 placed the former German city of Königsberg under the Soviet Union. When the USSR broke up in 1991, the region stayed with Russia.
Q: Why is Kaliningrad not connected to Russia?
A: Kaliningrad was cut off in 1991, when the Soviet Union collapsed and Lithuania became independent. To reach mainland Russia over land, you must cross at least two countries: Lithuania and then Belarus or Latvia.
Q: What was Kaliningrad called before?
A: Kaliningrad was called Königsberg and was German until 1945. It was renamed Kaliningrad on July 4, 1946, after Mikhail Kalinin.

Transcript:

This is Russia.
But this little piece? Also Russia.
Russia: Still me!
Kaliningrad. Stuck between Poland and Lithuania.
Until 1945, it was German: Königsberg.
Then the Soviets took it and renamed it.
In 1991 the USSR collapsed, Lithuania left… and Kaliningrad was cut off.
Russia: Hello?!
By 2004, both neighbours were in NATO and the EU.
Poland: Hi, neighbour!
Why keep it? It's Russia's only Baltic port that never freezes.
The catch? The rest of Russia is two countries away.

Sources: Potsdam Agreement (1945); NATO and EU accession records; US Naval Institute; DW

## Russia Sold Alaska for 2 Cents an Acre

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/alaska-sale/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i47FW9FEceQ
Published: 2026-11-22 · Duration: 0:37 · Place: Alaska
Short answer: Why did Russia sell Alaska? In 1867 it was hard to defend, far from St Petersburg and next door to British Canada, so Russia sold it to the United States for $7.2 million: about two cents an acre. Today Alaska pumps $7 million worth of oil every few hours.

Key facts:
- Purchase price: $7,200,000 (The sum the United States agreed to pay Russia for Alaska in 1867.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- Treaty signed: March 30, 1867 (Signed in Washington by US Secretary of State William Seward and Russian minister Eduard de Stoeckl, at 4 a.m. after negotiating through the night.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- Senate vote: 37 to 2 (The US Senate ratified the treaty on April 9, 1867.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- Formal handover: October 18, 1867 (In Sitka, the Russian flag was lowered and the US flag was raised.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- Price per acre: About 2 cents (Roughly 1,518,800 km² (375 million acres) for $7.2 million works out to about 1.9 cents an acre.)
- Size compared with France: About 2.7 times (Alaska has about 1,481,346 km² of land, against about 543,940 km² for metropolitan France.)
- Prudhoe Bay oil discovery: Announced March 12, 1968 (Prudhoe Bay is the largest oil field in the United States.) [source: National Park Service]
- Alaska oil output in 2026: About 413,000–428,000 barrels a day (At around $100 a barrel, that is roughly $7 million worth of oil every four hours.) [source: US Energy Information Administration]

### Why Russia Sold Alaska to the United States in 1867

Russia sold Alaska because it was hard to defend and Russia feared losing it to Britain in a future war. In 1867 it agreed to sell the territory to the United States for **$7.2 million**, about two cents an acre. Today Alaska produces that much money in oil every few hours.

## What was Alaska before 1867?

Before the sale, the land was a Russian colony known as *Russian America*. The name "Alaska" was chosen by the United States after the purchase.

It was enormous. Alaska has about 1,481,346 km² of land, roughly **2.7 times** the size of metropolitan France. The area covered by the treaty was about 1,518,800 km², or some 375 million acres.

## Why did Russia want to sell Alaska?

After its defeat in the Crimean War, Russia saw Alaska as difficult to defend. Historians point to one main concern: in a future war, British forces could take the territory easily from neighbouring Canada. In 1867 the land to the east, including the Yukon, was British territory.

According to the US Office of the Historian, selling to the United States was a way to offset the designs of Great Britain in the region. If Russia was going to lose Alaska, it preferred that the United States have it.

## How did the deal happen?

The treaty was negotiated by US Secretary of State **William Seward** and the Russian minister in Washington, **Eduard de Stoeckl**. After talks that ran through the night, they signed it in Washington at 4 a.m. on **March 30, 1867**.

The US Senate ratified it on **April 9, 1867**, by a vote of 37 to 2. The formal handover took place in **Sitka on October 18, 1867**, when the Russian flag came down and the US flag went up.

## How much did the United States pay?

The price was **$7,200,000**. Divided over roughly 375 million acres, that comes to about 1.9 cents an acre, or around two cents. Adjusted with the consumer price index, $7.2 million in 1867 is roughly **$164 million** in 2026 dollars.

## Was the Alaska Purchase called Seward's Folly?

Yes, by some. Critics dubbed it *Seward's Folly* and *Seward's Icebox*, mocking the idea of paying for a frozen land. Those nicknames stuck, but they did not reflect the whole picture: most of the press at the time supported the purchase.

## What happened after the sale?

First came gold. The first major strike in Alaska was at Anvil Creek, near Nome, on September 20, 1898, and the Nome gold rush ran from 1899 to 1909.

Then came oil. The discovery at **Prudhoe Bay** was announced on March 12, 1968. It is the largest oil field in the United States.

## How much oil does Alaska produce today?

In 2026 Alaska has been producing around 413,000 to 428,000 barrels a day, and Alaska North Slope crude has traded at around $100 or more. At about 420,000 barrels and $100 a barrel, that is roughly $42 million a day, or about $7.2 million every four hours. Even at much lower prices, such as $55 a barrel, it would take only around seven and a half hours.

So who got the better deal? Russia sold a territory it believed it could not hold. The United States bought land whose value only became clear decades later.

## Key takeaways

- Russia sold Alaska in 1867 because it was hard to defend and Russia feared losing it to Britain.
- The price was $7.2 million, about two cents an acre.
- The treaty was signed on March 30, 1867, and Alaska was handed over in Sitka on October 18, 1867.
- Critics called it *Seward's Folly*, though most of the press supported it.
- Gold near Nome and oil at Prudhoe Bay later made Alaska far more valuable than its purchase price.

FAQ:
Q: Why did Russia sell Alaska?
A: Russia sold Alaska because it was hard to defend and Russia feared British forces in Canada would take it in a future war. It preferred to sell it to the United States instead.
Q: How much did the US pay for Alaska?
A: The United States paid $7.2 million in 1867, about two cents an acre. That is roughly $164 million in 2026 dollars when adjusted for inflation.
Q: When did Alaska become part of the United States?
A: The purchase treaty was signed on March 30, 1867, and ratified by the Senate on April 9, 1867. The formal transfer took place in Sitka on October 18, 1867.

But it's hard to defend, and Russia fears Britain will grab it.
So it offers a deal to the United States.

United States: Deal!
That's two cents an acre.
Critics call it Seward's Folly… a giant icebox.
Then come gold… and oil.
Today, Alaska pumps seven million dollars of oil every few hours.
And to think…

Sources: US Office of the Historian; National Park Service; US Energy Information Administration; Alaska Department of Revenue

## How Much of Ukraine Does Russia Control?

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/ukraine-front/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FRN2bWGVwTU
Published: 2026-11-21 · Duration: 0:37 · Place: Ukraine
Short answer: How much of Ukraine does Russia control? About 19% in November 2026, according to DeepStateMap: roughly 114,000 km², an area bigger than Portugal. We rewind the map to 2013 and watch the front line move, month by month.

Key facts:
- Share of Ukraine controlled by Russia (17 Nov 2026): About 19% (19.2% of Ukraine including Crimea, based on the DeepStateMap snapshot of 17 November 2026.) [source: DeepStateMap (deepstatemap.live), monthly snapshots to 17 Nov 2026]
- Area controlled by Russia (17 Nov 2026): About 114,000 km² (114,449 km² in the 17 November 2026 snapshot, more than the whole of Portugal (92,225 km²).) [source: DeepStateMap (deepstatemap.live), monthly snapshots to 17 Nov 2026]
- Annexation of Crimea: 18 March 2014 (The date the treaty annexing Crimea to Russia was signed.) [source: Britannica]
- Fighting in the Donbas: April 2014 (Russian troops and Russian-backed local forces took part of the Donbas; the line there was stable from February 2015.) [source: Britannica]
- Full-scale invasion: 24 February 2022 (Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.) [source: Britannica]
- Peak of Russian control (March 2022): Over a fifth (Estimates range from about 21% (around 133,000 km²) to 27% depending on the source.) [source: ISW]
- Share controlled by Russia (December 2022): 17.7% (After Ukraine retook ground around Kyiv, Kharkiv and Kherson in 2022, the figure rose slowly to 19.2% by November 2026.) [source: DeepStateMap (deepstatemap.live), monthly snapshots to 17 Nov 2026]

### Ukraine's Front Line from 2014 to 2026, Month by Month

As of 17 November 2026, Russia controls about 19% of Ukraine, according to DeepStateMap: roughly 114,000 km², including Crimea. That is an area larger than the whole of Portugal. The figure is the result of more than a decade of change, from the annexation of Crimea in 2014 to the full-scale invasion of 2022 and the slow movement of the front line since.

*All front-line figures on this page refer to the date given. The line keeps moving, so later figures may differ.*

## How much of Ukraine does Russia control today?

In the DeepStateMap snapshot of 17 November 2026, Russia controlled 114,449 km², or 19.2% of Ukraine including Crimea. Measured against Ukraine's official area of 603,550 km², the share is 19.0%.

Other trackers give similar figures. Russia Matters, using DeepStateMap data to 11 November 2026, put it at about 45,227 square miles, roughly 117,100 km², or "about 19% of Ukraine". The Council on Foreign Relations' Global Conflict Tracker describes it as roughly 20 percent.

For scale: Portugal covers 92,225 km² including its islands. The area under Russian control in November 2026 is larger than all of it.

## What happened in 2014?

In 2013, the whole of Ukraine, including Crimea, was under Ukrainian control. That changed in 2014.

- **March 2014:** Russia annexed Crimea. The annexation treaty was signed on 18 March 2014.
- **April 2014:** Russian troops and Russian-backed local forces took control of part of the Donbas, in eastern Ukraine.
- **February 2015:** after the fighting around Debaltseve, the line in the Donbas became largely stable.

## What changed in 2022?

On 24 February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with forces advancing from the north, the east and the south.

Russian control peaked in March 2022. Estimates of that peak vary by source, from about 21% of the country (around 133,000 km², according to ISW) to 27% (according to Al Jazeera). Either way, Russia held over a fifth of Ukraine at that point.

## Where did Ukraine retake territory?

Ukraine pushed back in three main areas during 2022:

- **Around Kyiv:** Russian forces withdrew from the north in April 2022.
- **Around Kharkiv:** a Ukrainian counteroffensive in September 2022 retook ground in the region.
- **Around Kherson:** Ukraine retook Kherson on 11 November 2022.

By December 2022, the share of Ukraine under Russian control had fallen to 17.7%.

## How has the front line moved since 2023?

Since then, the changes have been gradual. Month by month, Russian forces have advanced slowly, village by village, notably on the Donetsk front. The share of Ukraine under Russian control rose from 17.7% in December 2022 to 19.2% in November 2026.

The front line is still moving, which is why every figure on this page is tied to a date.

## Key takeaways

- As of 17 November 2026, Russia controls about 19% of Ukraine (114,449 km², including Crimea), according to DeepStateMap.
- That area is larger than Portugal (92,225 km²).
- Russia annexed Crimea in March 2014; Russian-backed forces took part of the Donbas the same year.
- The full-scale invasion began on 24 February 2022; at its peak in March 2022, Russia held over a fifth of the country.
- Ukraine retook ground around Kyiv, Kharkiv and Kherson in 2022, bringing the figure to 17.7% by December 2022.
- Since then, the share has risen slowly to 19.2% by November 2026.

Q: When did Russia annex Crimea?
A: In March 2014. The annexation treaty was signed on 18 March 2014, and in April 2014 Russian-backed forces also took part of the Donbas.
Q: What was the most territory Russia held in Ukraine?
A: Over a fifth of the country, at the peak in March 2022, shortly after the full-scale invasion of 24 February 2022. Estimates range from about 21% to 27% depending on the source.

## The True Size of Africa: US, India and EU Fit

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/africa-size/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6WHdqIvEl5o
Published: 2026-11-20 · Duration: 0:36 · Place: Africa
Short answer: What is the true size of Africa? On a Mercator map Greenland looks just as big, but Africa is 14 times larger: the mainland US, India and all 27 EU countries fit inside it at the same time, with almost half the continent to spare.

Key facts:
- Area of Africa: About 30.4 million km² (Estimates range from 30,365,000 to 30,370,000 km² depending on the source.) [source: Britannica]
- Area of Greenland: 2,166,086 km² (On a Mercator map Greenland looks about as big as Africa.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Africa compared with Greenland: 14 times bigger (Africa's area divided by Greenland's comes out at about 14.) [source: Britannica]
- Mercator projection: 1569 (Drawn by Gerardus Mercator for navigators; it enlarges areas about 4 times at 60° latitude and about 10.5 times at 72°.)
- Mainland United States: 8,080,464 km² (The 48 contiguous states plus DC, without Alaska or Hawaii.) [source: US Census Bureau]
- India: 3,287,263 km² (The second country placed inside Africa in the comparison.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- European Union (27 countries): 4,236,351 km² (All 27 member states fit inside Africa together with the US and India.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Share of Africa still uncovered: Almost half (The three together cover 15,604,078 km², about 51% of Africa, leaving about 49% free.) [source: fit measured on Natural Earth outlines]

### Mercator vs Reality: How Big Africa Actually Is

Africa covers about 30.4 million km², roughly 14 times the area of Greenland, even though the two look about the same size on the world map most people know. Africa is so large that the mainland United States, India and all 27 countries of the European Union fit inside it at the same time, and almost half of the continent is still left uncovered.

## Why does Africa look smaller than it is?

The map most of us grew up with uses the Mercator projection, drawn by Gerardus Mercator in 1569 for navigators. To flatten a round globe into a rectangle, it stretches everything that lies far from the equator.

The stretching grows fast as you move towards the poles. At 60 degrees of latitude, areas look about 4 times bigger than they really are. At 72 degrees, they look about 10.5 times bigger.

Mercator has never gone away. Online maps such as Google Maps use a version of it called Web Mercator, so it is still the picture of the world many people see every day.

Africa lies across the equator, where Mercator distorts least. Greenland, Canada and Russia lie far to the north, where it distorts most.

## Is Greenland really as big as Africa?

No. On a Mercator map Greenland looks about as big as Africa, but that is the projection at work.

Greenland covers 2,166,086 km². Africa covers about 30.4 million km². Divide one by the other and you get roughly 14. Slide Greenland down to the equator, where the map stops stretching it, and it shrinks into a small patch inside Africa.

## What countries fit inside Africa?

To show how big Africa really is, we placed three large pieces of the world inside it, all at once and without overlapping:

- **The mainland United States:** 8,080,464 km², meaning the 48 contiguous states plus DC, without Alaska or Hawaii.
- **India:** 3,287,263 km².
- **The European Union:** 4,236,351 km² across all 27 member states.

Together they add up to 15,604,078 km², about 51% of Africa. That leaves roughly 49% of the continent, almost half, still uncovered.

## How was the fit checked?

The comparison is not an artist's sketch. The fit was measured on Natural Earth outlines, moving each country across the globe without stretching or distorting its shape, only allowing it to rotate.

A few choices keep it fair:

- Africa means the mainland only, without Madagascar, small islands or the Sinai Peninsula.
- The United States means the 48 contiguous states.
- India is shown without the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
- EU countries are shown with their European territory only, without the Canary Islands, the Azores, Madeira or overseas regions.

With those outlines, all 29 pieces fit inside mainland Africa with 0 km² sticking out past the coast and 0 km² of overlap between them.

## Key takeaways

- Africa covers about 30.4 million km², around 14 times the size of Greenland.
- The Mercator projection (1569) stretches land far from the equator, which is why Greenland looks as big as Africa.
- The mainland US, India and all 27 EU countries fit inside Africa at the same time.
- Those three together cover about 51% of Africa, leaving almost half uncovered.
- The fit was measured on real outlines, with no overlap and nothing outside the coast.

FAQ:
Q: How much bigger is Africa than Greenland?
A: About 14 times bigger. Africa covers about 30.4 million km² and Greenland 2,166,086 km², even though they look similar on a Mercator map.
Q: Why does Greenland look so big on maps?
A: Because most world maps use the Mercator projection, which stretches everything far from the equator. At 60° latitude areas look about 4 times larger than they really are, and at 72° about 10.5 times larger.
Q: Can the US, India and Europe fit inside Africa?
A: Yes. The mainland US, India and all 27 EU countries fit inside Africa at the same time, without overlapping, and almost half of the continent is still left uncovered.

Transcript:

It's called Mercator. To flatten the globe, it stretches everything near the poles.
So Greenland looks as big as Africa.
Now slide it down to the equator.
Africa is fourteen times bigger.
So what fits inside? The mainland US…
United States: Wait. I'm the small one?
India…
…and the entire EU. All 27 countries, at once.
And almost half of Africa is still uncovered.
So next time you see this map…

Sources: Britannica; CIA World Factbook; US Census Bureau; fit measured on Natural Earth outlines

## Lesotho: The Country Inside South Africa

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/lesotho/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJLDw3Rc5ns
Published: 2026-11-19 · Duration: 0:36 · Place: Lesotho
Short answer: Why is Lesotho inside South Africa? It's a whole independent country, about the size of Belgium, completely surrounded by a single neighbour. Even its lowest point sits 1,400 metres above sea level: a world record.

Key facts:
- Area of Lesotho: 30,355 km² (A fully independent country, completely surrounded by South Africa.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Area of Belgium, for comparison: 30,689 km² (Lesotho and Belgium are almost exactly the same size.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Lowest point in Lesotho: About 1,400 m (The highest lowest point of any country in the world.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- British protection: 1868 (King Moshoeshoe I asked Britain for protection, and the territory became the protectorate of Basutoland.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Union of South Africa: 1910 (Basutoland stayed outside the Union of South Africa and never joined it.)
- Independence: 4 October 1966 (Basutoland became the independent country of Lesotho.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Countries entirely surrounded by one other country: 3 (Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City.)

### How Lesotho Ended Up Surrounded by South Africa

Lesotho is inside South Africa because of a decision taken more than 150 years ago. It is a fully independent country of 30,355 km², about the size of Belgium, and South Africa surrounds it completely. In 1868 its king asked Britain for protection; in 1910 the territory, then called Basutoland, stayed outside the Union of South Africa; and on 4 October 1966 it became independent as Lesotho.

## Where exactly is Lesotho?

Look at a map of southern Africa and you will spot a hole in the middle of South Africa. That hole is not a lake or a nature reserve. It is a separate country with its own government and its own borders: Lesotho.

What makes it unusual is that it has only one neighbour. Every kilometre of its border is shared with South Africa. Geographers call this an enclave: a country entirely surrounded by a single other country.

## How big is Lesotho?

Lesotho covers 30,355 km². Belgium covers 30,689 km². The two are almost exactly the same size.

So Lesotho is not a tiny city-state tucked into a corner of the map. It is a country the size of a European nation, sitting completely inside its larger neighbour.

## Why is Lesotho's lowest point a world record?

Lesotho holds a genuine world record. Its lowest point is about 1,400 metres above sea level, the highest lowest point of any country on Earth.

In practical terms, there is nowhere in Lesotho that sits lower than roughly 1,400 metres. Even the bottom of the country is high ground: the whole of Lesotho sits well above sea level.

## Why did Lesotho never become part of South Africa?

The answer is in its history. Three dates explain most of it:

- **1868:** King Moshoeshoe I asked Britain for protection. The territory became the British protectorate of Basutoland.
- **1910:** The Union of South Africa came together, and Basutoland stayed outside it.
- **4 October 1966:** Basutoland became independent and took the name Lesotho.

British protection put Basutoland on a separate track from its neighbours. When the Union of South Africa was formed in 1910, Basutoland was not part of it, and it never joined afterwards. By the time it became independent in 1966, the borders were already set. The result is the map we see today: an independent country with a single neighbour on every side.

## Are there other countries completely surrounded by another country?

Yes, but very few. Only three countries on Earth are entirely surrounded by one other country. Lesotho is one of them. The other two are San Marino and Vatican City.

That makes Lesotho a true geographic rarity: one of just three countries in the world that cannot reach any other nation without first crossing a single neighbour.

## Key takeaways

- Lesotho is an independent country completely surrounded by South Africa.
- It covers 30,355 km², about the same as Belgium (30,689 km²).
- Its lowest point is about 1,400 metres above sea level, a world record.
- In 1868 King Moshoeshoe I asked Britain for protection, creating Basutoland.
- Basutoland stayed outside the Union of South Africa in 1910 and became independent as Lesotho on 4 October 1966.
- Only three countries are surrounded by a single country: Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City.

FAQ:
Q: Why is Lesotho inside South Africa?
A: Because of its history: in 1868 its king, Moshoeshoe I, asked Britain for protection, and the territory became Basutoland. It stayed outside the Union of South Africa in 1910 and became independent as Lesotho in 1966, still surrounded on every side by South Africa.
Q: How big is Lesotho compared to Belgium?
A: They are almost the same size. Lesotho covers 30,355 km² and Belgium covers 30,689 km².
Q: Which countries are completely surrounded by another country?
A: Only three: Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City. Lesotho is the one surrounded by South Africa.
